en: Annotated Commentary on the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* Spoken by the Buddha.

Compiled by the Chan Master Yongxiang, who received imperial authorization to preach at the Imperial Altar, was bestowed with purple robes, and granted a golden Buddha and a jeweled crown; supplemented by Guling Liaotong.
△ To explain the outline of the commentary on this sutra, it is divided into four parts. First, the explanation of the title of the sutra.

Within this single title, *The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha in Forty-two Sections*, there is both person and dharma, as well as the agent and the object. It is a dual title comprising both person and dharma, and both agent and object.
Closing the eyes. Therefore it is called *The Sutra of Forty-two Sections Spoken by the Buddha*. This is the general title; what follows is the specific explanation.

Regarding "Spoken by the Buddha": this refers to the proclamation from the golden mouth of our Buddha, who, employing unimpeded eloquence, expounded the wondrous Dharma that accords with the capacities of beings;
hence it is called "Spoken by the Buddha. Furthermore, "Buddha" is a Sanskrit term (*buddha*), which in the language of China means "the Awakened One."
One of the Ten Epithets [of a Buddha]. To have ultimately awakened to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is called "Perfect Enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*).
Furthermore, "to speak" (*śāsana*) means "to gladden. Speaking in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings accords with the Buddha’s intent;

that is to say, he vibrates the perfect sound to awaken the multitudes and proclaims the wondrous meaning to harmonize with their capacities—thus, it is called "speaking. Regarding the "Forty-two Sections": *zhāng* (sections) refers to chapters. This refers to...

The scripture consists of forty-two chapters. It is intended to cause every person to abandon evil destinies and cultivate goodness, to sever hindrances and eliminate delusions, to transcend the mundane and enter the sacred, and to reach the shore of Bodhi;
hence it is titled the "Forty-two Chapters. As for the term "sūtra" (jīng), it fully signifies the constant Dharma that threads through and encompasses all.

This means it threads through the principles and meanings while encompassing the appropriate capacities of those to be transformed. It does not shift across the three periods of time, and the ten realms follow its same track. Therefore...
This constitutes a sūtra. Therefore, the Buddha is the person; the Forty-two Sections are the Dharma. The single character "sūtra" (jīng) is the expressive text (*vācaka*);
the preceding six characters are the expressed meaning (*vācya*). Thus, the person and the Dharma are presented together as the title, and the expresser and the expressed are combined in the name.
Hence, it is called *The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha in Forty-two Sections*.
△ Second, the period of the translators:
Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna translated [the scriptures] together during the Later Han.
"Later" (Hou) is said in contrast to the preceding [Han], and it is also called Eastern Han; this refers to the time of Emperor Ming of the Han, specifically the seventh year of the Yongping era.
In the [first] year of the reign, the Emperor dreamed of a golden man, sixteen feet in height, with a halo around his neck like the sun, who arrived through the air and circled the palace courtyard.
He pointed to the Emperor’s throne and said, "The establishment of the Teaching. At dawn, the Emperor questioned his ministers. Then Fu Yi submitted a memorial, saying:
"According to my consultation of the *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Record of Marvels in the Book of Zhou), in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of Zhou, the Jia-yin year, the fourth month..."
On the eighth day, at the hour of the rat, auspicious light of five colors pierced through the Taiwei Palace. At that time, the King questioned his ministers as to the reason for this.
The Grand Astrologer Suyou replied, "In the West, a Great Sage has been born.
A thousand years hence, his teachings shall flow into this land. That which Your Majesty dreamed must surely be of him. The next day, it was indeed so.
He dispatched eighteen men, including Qin Jing, Cai Yin, and Wang Zun, to travel together to the Western Regions to seek out [the Dharma].
Upon reaching the kingdom of Yuezhi, they encountered the two Indian monks, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna.

These monks were carrying one scroll of a painted image of Śākyamuni Buddha, as well as the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*, the *Ten Stages Sūtra on Severing the Bonds*, and other texts. They returned with these items, having transported them on white horses.

In Luoyang, the land of Han, on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month in the tenth year of the Yongping era, [Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna] were presented and admitted into the palace gates to offer a golden Buddha image.
Emperor Ming was greatly delighted and lodged them at the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglù sì).

The Emperor then issued a decree to establish a monastery outside the Yong Gate to the west of the city, which was also named the Court of State Ceremonial Monastery. Consequently, there were the Daoist practitioners of the Five Peaks, Chǔ Shànxìn and Fèi Zhǔ.
Cai and his colleagues submitted a memorial to the throne, stating: "Your Majesty does not believe the words of the Chinese people, but instead believes the speech of the barbarians.
We shall take the scriptures with him and burn them to test their authenticity. If we prevail, we shall exile the Hu man to the remote borderlands;
if he prevails, we shall sever our own heads. The Emperor approved this petition and consequently ordered the burning of the scriptures.
The platform was prepared, and the supernatural powers were put to the test.

Although figures such as Chu had frequently displayed miraculous transformations—such as riding upon grass-dragons to ascend into the air or traveling back and forth through the void—when it came time to burn the scriptures at the foot of the platform, the Daoist texts were entirely reduced to ashes.
Only Yin Xi managed to snatch the *Daode jing* and the *Zhuangzi* from the midst of the flames; all the others were completely consumed by the fire. Chu...
They were likewise unable to fly up and descend or travel back and forth; their supernatural powers had all vanished.
The Buddha image and the Buddhist scriptures then transformed into lotus flowers and surged upward into the air, without being damaged by even a hair’s breadth.
Once the Daoists were defeated, some hanged themselves, some shaved their heads, and some threw themselves into wells. The heads and eyes of those such as Chu were all cut off.

[The Emperor] said, and so forth. The Emperor subsequently issued an imperial decree changing the name of the Honglu (Court of State Ceremonial) to Baima Si (White Horse Monastery). An Shigao established the Buddha images;
Kāśyapa Mātanga and Zhu Falan resided there and translated various sutras, and so forth.
△ Third, the annotation of the title.
Annotated by the śramaṇa Shousui, successor to the patriarchs at the Fengshan Aranya in Yunjiao, Song.
"Yunjiao" refers to the Yunyang Prefecture in Huguang. "Fengshan" (Phoenix Mountain) was named after its physical form; this mountain...
"Resembling a phoenix" is also the name of the mountain itself. "Āraṇya" is a Sanskrit term; here it means a "place of tranquility.
"Successor to the Patriarchs" refers to one who inherits the position of the Buddhas and Patriarchs from their predecessors. "Śramaṇa" is a Sanskrit term; here it means "diligent cessation.
This refers to diligently cultivating precepts, concentration, and wisdom, while ceasing and extinguishing greed, hatred, and delusion; therefore, they are called śramaṇas.

"Superior guarding and inferior fulfillment"—this is the name of the Master. Regarding the term "commentary" (zhù): it is said that when there is a presiding authority at the margins, it is called a commentary;
furthermore, it is called a commentary because it divides the text and analyzes its meaning.
△ Fourth, the explanation of the main text of the sutra, in two parts. First, the introduction by the scribe, in three sections. First, the account of the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment:
After the World-Honored One had attained the Way, he reflected thus: "Seclusion from desire and tranquility are the most supreme.
Abiding in great meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), he subdued all the paths of Māra.
△ Second, the sequence of transmitting the Dharma and delivering sentient beings:
In the Deer Park, he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths and delivered the five men, including Kauṇḍinya, who thereby realized the fruits of the Path.

The Dharma-body of the pure realm is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; yet, through the power of great compassion and vows, it manifests birth and attains enlightenment through the eight phases—this is the Buddha-jewel.
Contemplating skillful means, one abandons desire as the precepts; from this arises meditative concentration which engenders wisdom;

thus one subdues Māra, reveals the truth, turns the wheel of Dharma, and delivers sentient beings—this is the Dharma-jewel. The Four Truths refer to suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; these constitute two levels: the ultimate and the conventional.

Regarding cause and effect, there are differences in magnitude according to the faculties through which one practices and realizes the path. When the Buddha first left home and practiced the Way in the Snowy Mountains, King Śuddhodana sent three members of his clan:
first, Aśvajit; second, Bhadrika; and [third, Mahānāman]. As for the group of five including Kauṇḍinya, they were those with whom the Buddha first attained realization.
There were three Mahānāmas and two maternal uncles: one was Kauṇḍinya and the other was Daśabala-Kāśyapa.
These five followed and protected [the Buddha], but later they each departed for the Deer Park, where they collectively practiced heterodox paths.

When the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment, he first turned the Wheel of Dharma for them three times, and all five attained the realization of the fruits of the path; this was the beginning of the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
△ Third: Requesting Instruction by Resolving Doubts.
Furthermore, there were various doubts concerning what certain bhikṣus had said; they sought the Buddha’s guidance. The World-Honored One instructed them, awakening each one to understanding.
With palms joined in reverence, he accepted and followed the Honored One’s command.
*Bhikṣu*—in the Song language, it is sometimes called "upholder of pure precepts," sometimes called "destroyer of afflictions," and sometimes called "pure beggar."

It is also called "Able to Terrify Māra. This single name in India encompasses these four meanings; therefore, the translator retained the meaning in the title. With doubts and questions, one requests instruction;
according to the ailment, the remedy is prescribed. Through faith and awakening, one attains peace; through reverence and compliance, it is propagated.
In the past, after the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa, a thousand years passed. During the Yongping era of the Later Han, Emperor Ming, due to a dream of a golden image, [sought the Dharma].

It was then known that the Buddhist teachings were about to reach the Eastern Land. Emperor Ming dispatched Cai Yin as an envoy to the Western Regions, where he encountered two Indian monks, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna.
Carrying on white horses the *palm-leaf* Sanskrit manuscripts, they arrived at the capital of Luoyang and translated the Sanskrit texts into Chinese.
This sutra stands foremost, its teachings revealed in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; it is the most essential, concise in expression yet complete in meaning.

The introductory section and the section on circulation have been presented above. The following forty-two chapters clarify the profound intent of abandoning evil destinies and cultivating goodness, eliminating delusions and severing hindrances, thereby transcending the mundane and entering the state of sagehood.
△ Section Two: The Direct Proclamation from the Golden Mouth, divided into forty-two parts. First: Leaving Home and Realizing the Fruit. The Buddha said:
"One who leaves home to renounce kin, recognizes the mind and penetrates the fundamental source, and understands the unconditioned Dharma (*asamskṛta-dharma*), is called a śramaṇa.
Constantly practicing the two hundred and fifty precepts, with conduct and movement pure, they cultivate the four true paths of practice and become an arhat. Arhat...
The Han are those who can fly and undergo transformations, possess lifespans spanning vast kalpas, and cause heaven and earth to shake.
Next are the Anāgāmins; when their lives end, their spirits ascend to the nineteenth heaven.
From the two realms of desire and form up to the Heaven of Non-conception, there are nineteen heavens in total.

Those above these are the five heavens of the Non-returners (Anāgāmin), who realize Arhatship. Next are the Once-returners (Sakṛdāgāmin); a Once-returner goes up once and returns once more before attaining Arhatship.
Next are the Stream-enterers (Srotāpanna); a Stream-enterer undergoes seven deaths and seven births before realizing Arhatship.
One who has severed craving is like one whose four limbs have been severed; they can no longer be used.

"Śramaṇa" (沙門) is translated in the Song language as "one who exerts himself in practice. To exert oneself in practice is to advance toward Nirvāṇa. Within the cycle of the three realms, craving is the cause.
To sever craving and bid farewell to kin is the renunciation of the body. To realize the mind and reach its fundamental source is the renunciation of the mind.

There are three kinds of renunciation: first, leaving one's kin and departing from the secular household; second, awakening to the Way and departing from the household of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*);

third, realizing the fruit and departing from the household of the three realms (*tridhātu*). Among the two hundred and fifty precepts of a great *bhikṣu*, the four acts of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying constitute the root.
All other branches and leaves arise in dependence upon these four fundamental laws. If one violates the root...
If the root is present but the branches and twigs are difficult to produce, there will be no means by which to realize the fruit.

If one strictly maintains each precept without transgression, then according to the various stages of the afflictions abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), the realizations attained will accordingly differ. This refers to the first fruit, *srotāpanna*.

The second fruit is the *Srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer); Songyun translates this as "entering the stream. The third fruit is the *Sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner); Songyun translates this as "one who returns once," meaning one returns once to the heavens and once to the human realm before realizing *nirvāṇa*.
The fourth fruit is the *Anāgāmin* (Non-returner); Songyun translates this as "not returning. The fifth fruit is the *Arhat*; Songyun translates this as "non-arising.
With afflictions completely severed, they have already realized the emptiness of birth (*jātisūnyatā*). It is like having one's four limbs severed; [they are no longer subject to rebirth].
This is the unconditioned fruit.
△ Second, severing desire and extinguishing its traces.

The Buddha said: "Those who have left the household life as śramaṇas cut off desire and abandon attachment; they recognize the source of their own minds, penetrate the profound principle of the Buddhas, and awaken."
Regarding unconditioned dharmas:
when one penetrates the source, emotions vanish; when one realizes the essence of the mind, it merges with its true nature.
Internally there is nothing to be attained, and externally there is nothing to be sought. The mind is neither bound to the Way nor does it form karmic bonds.
Externally, it severs all攀緣 (pān-yuan, objective attachments); internally, it does not maintain stillness.
It is without thought and without action; it is neither cultivation nor realization.
It is a single mark and a single practice, without realization and without attainment.
Without passing through the various stages, one spontaneously attains the highest honor; this is what is called the Way.
Its numinous mechanism is beyond all traces—how could it be contained within a hierarchy?
△ Third: Severing Attachment and Eliminating Greed.
The Buddha said: "One who shaves off hair and beard to become a śramaṇa and receives the Way’s Dharma leaves behind worldly wealth and possessions, seeking only enough to satisfy one's needs.
By shaving off hair and beard, one quiets craving; by casting away wealth and possessions, one abandons greed."
Eat but one meal at midday; lodge but one night under a tree; be careful not to do these again.
These are the supreme practices of the dhūta ascetic, free from attachment and clinging.
That which causes people to be deluded and obscured is craving and desire.
Obscured by darkness and delusion, brought about by craving and desire.
△ Fourth, the clarification of both good and evil.
The Buddha said: "Sentient beings take ten matters as good, and likewise take ten matters as evil. What are these ten? [The first is] the body..."

Three of the mouth, four of the mind, and three of the body: the three of the body are killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; the four of the mouth are double-tongued speech, harsh speech, lying, and frivolous speech;
the three of the mind are envy, malice, and delusion. These ten matters are contrary to the Noble Path and are called the ten unwholesome actions.
If these evils cease, they are merely called the ten virtuous actions.
The natures of good and evil are empty, like the turning of one's palm. To cease evil and practice good is to follow the Noble Path.

Since the self-nature is fundamentally without killing, one observes the precept of non-killing; likewise, since the self-nature is fundamentally without greed, hatred, and delusion, one observes the precepts of non-greed and so forth.

The eighty-four thousand afflictions are transformed into the gates of the *pāramitās*. According to the capacities of beings, they are differentiated into superior, middling, and inferior grades, as fully recorded in the Great Sūtras.
△ Five: Transforming the heavy into the light.

The Buddha said: "If a person has many transgressions yet does not repent, and fails to suddenly still the mind, then sin will come upon the person like water flowing to the sea, gradually becoming deep and vast."

The beginning of transgression is as slight as the overflow of a stream, yet its ultimate calamity is like being submerged to the crown of the head. If one’s evil intent does not cease, the ocean of karma becomes ever deeper.
Should a person commit a fault, if they understand their error and recognize it for themselves, reforming their wickedness and practicing virtue, their sins will naturally be extinguished.
To reform one's errors and renew oneself, sins perish along with the mind;
it is like a patient who, upon breaking a sweat, gradually finds relief from their ailment.
As the body becomes at ease when a patient sweats, so the mind becomes pure when a person reforms their faults.
△ Sixth, enduring evil without anger.
The Buddha said: "If wicked people hear of the good and come to cause disturbance, you should restrain yourself and remain free from anger or reproach.
It is they who come with evil intent who are themselves the ones who are evil."
He has already attained equanimity; why be angry when provoked? By viewing enemies and kin with equal regard, Māra will naturally retreat and be humiliated.
△ Seventh, the evil ones return to their original forms.
The Buddha said: "There were those who, hearing that I maintain the Way and practice great benevolence and compassion, came to revile the Buddha. The Buddha remained silent and did not respond."
The abuse ceased. [The Buddha] asked, "If you follow someone with courtesy and that person does not accept it, does the courtesy return to you? He replied, "It does.
The Buddha said, "Now you have reviled me, and I do not accept it; you yourself shall carry the calamity back upon your own person."
By the power of the roots of merit from practicing charity, even if one were to employ worldly metaphors to revile the Buddha, one would bring calamity upon oneself.
This principle is as manifest as an echo following a sound or a shadow following a form; there is ultimately no way to escape it. Be careful not to do evil.
Body and speech are driven by the mind; their influence is difficult to escape.
△ Eighth: Dust and spittle defile themselves. The Buddha said:
"When a wicked person harms a virtuous one, it is like looking up at the sky and spitting. The spittle does not reach the sky; it falls back upon oneself."
When wind blows against it, dust does not reach its destination; instead, it returns to soil one's own body. The worthy cannot be defamed; disaster will surely destroy the slanderer.

To harm the worthy invites retribution, like spitting at heaven or throwing dust upward—the dust falls back and soils oneself. In the past, when a singer sang of his grievances against the Buddha, the Buddha felt no anger or resentment and attained perfect enlightenment.
Once the singer’s transgressions were exhausted, he encountered the Buddha and received a prediction of his future Buddhahood.
△ Ninth, the Assembly on Returning to the Source.
The Buddha said: "To love the Way through extensive learning makes the Way difficult to realize.
Worldly wisdom, eloquence, and cleverness, as well as extensive learning and powerful memory, increase one's pride; thus, one remains far removed from the Way."
Guarding one's resolve and upholding the Way, that Way is exceedingly vast.
Firmly maintaining one's will and embodying the Way, its measure encompasses the entire Dharma-realm.
△ Tenth: Rejoicing in the Merit of Giving.
The Buddha said: "When one sees another person practicing giving on the Path, to assist them with joy brings forth exceedingly great merit.
Giving is the foremost of the myriad practices; if even assisting in joy yields such results, how much more so the merit of the act of giving itself?"
A śramaṇa asked, "Is this merit exhausted? The Buddha said, "It is like a single torch of fire;
if hundreds or thousands of people each come with their own torches to take a portion from it to cook food and dispel the darkness, that original torch remains as it was. Merit is just like this."
When fire meets a torch, the work of fire is inexhaustible; when blessings follow the mind, the retribution of blessings is endless.
△ Eleven: The Superiority of Giving Food.
The Buddha said: "To feed a hundred evil people is not as good as feeding one virtuous person. To feed a thousand virtuous people is not as good as feeding one..."

Feeding ten thousand persons who observe the five precepts is not equal to feeding one *srotāpanna*. Feeding one million *srotāpannas* is not equal to feeding one *sakṛdāgāmin*. Feeding ten million *sakṛdāgāmins* is not equal to feeding one *anāgāmin*. Feeding one hundred million *anāgāmins* is not equal to feeding one *arhat*. Feeding one billion *arhats*... [is not equal to feeding one... *pratyekabuddha*. Feeding ten billion *pratyekabuddhas* is not equal to feeding one *tathāgata*, arhat, perfectly enlightened Buddha. Feeding one hundred billion *tathāgatas*, arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas is not equal to building a stūpa for the relics of a *tathāgata*, arhat, perfectly enlightened Buddha. Building ten hundred billion stūpas for the relics of a *tathāgata*, arhat, perfectly enlightened Buddha is not equal to establishing a single lamp within that stūpa. Establishing ten hundred billion lamps within that stūpa is not equal to establishing a single wick within that stūpa. Establishing ten hundred billion wicks within that stūpa is not equal to establishing a single vessel of oil within that stūpa. Establishing ten hundred billion vessels of oil within that stūpa is not equal to establishing a single vessel of incense within that stūpa. Establishing ten hundred billion vessels of incense within that stūpa is not equal to establishing a single vessel of flowers within that stūpa. Establishing ten hundred billion vessels of flowers within that stūpa is not equal to establishing a single vessel of perfumed paste within that stūpa. Establishing ten hundred billion vessels of *sphatika* within that stūpa is not equal to establishing a single vessel of *musāragalva* within that stūpa. Establishing

O Han, it is not as good as providing a meal for one *pratyekabuddha*. Providing a meal for ten billion *pratyekabuddhas* is not as good as providing a meal for one Buddha of the three periods of time.

Providing a meal for a thousand billion Buddhas of the three periods of time is not as good as providing a meal for one who is without thought, without dwelling, without cultivation, and without realization.

Above, by selecting fields and sowing seeds, the disparity between excellence and inferiority increases tenfold. Dwelling upon appearances while seeking retribution further nourishes the root of craving;

as soon as the mind gives rise to thoughts and movements, it deviates from the essence of the Dharma. Now, since there is no thought, no dwelling, no cultivation, and no realization, the emotions of grasping and rejecting perish, and the three spheres are empty and still.
This is also as Vimalakīrti said: "If a donor gives with an impartial mind..."
Even the lowliest beggar is like the Tathāgata’s field of merit: free from discrimination, equal in great compassion, and seeking no reward.
This is what is meant by being fully endowed with the gift of Dharma; such is the meaning.
△ Twelfth: Raising Objections and Encouraging Practice.

The Buddha said: "There are twenty difficulties for human beings: it is difficult to practice giving when poor; it is difficult to study the Way when wealthy and noble; it is difficult to cast off one's life when facing certain death;

it is difficult to encounter the Buddha’s sutras; it is difficult to be born during the time of a Buddha; it is difficult to endure the temptations of form and desire; it is difficult to see what is beautiful..."

It is difficult to seek [the Way]. It is difficult not to become angry when insulted. It is difficult not to exercise power when one possesses it. It is difficult to remain free from mental attachment in all affairs.

It is difficult to study extensively and investigate deeply. It is difficult to eliminate the pride of self (*māna*). It is difficult not to look down upon those who have not yet studied. It is difficult for the mind’s conduct to be impartial. It is difficult not to speak of right or wrong.

It is difficult to encounter virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). It is difficult to realize one's nature and study the Path. It is difficult to transform and deliver others according to their needs. It is difficult not to be [distracted] by encountering external objects...
It is difficult to act; it is difficult to skillfully understand the means (*upāya*).
Difficult matters are numerous; they have been briefly opened up as above. To follow one’s own emotions is easy; to oppose one’s own will is difficult.
If one follows principle while opposing emotion, one may even cast aside one’s life to act. If one follows emotion while turning one’s back on principle, even if one sees—
To like [the Dharma] yet not seek it; to have power yet not exercise it; to maintain equanimity in thought and conduct; to love extensive learning yet remain humble;

to see those who have not yet studied yet not despise them; to practice *dāna* according to one's means despite being poor; and to turn one’s light inward to study the Way despite being wealthy and noble.

Knowing the faults and afflictions of form and desire, awakening to the perversity of right and wrong, one is further able to remain mindless when encountering sensory objects and skillfully understands expedient means.
Constantly associating with virtuous friends, one follows their transformative influence to deliver others. Everywhere one encounters the appearance of Buddhas in the world;

in every thought-moment, one turns the great scroll of the Dharma. Through its application, one accomplishes the great practices of a Bodhisattva, and through its manifestation, one enters immeasurable subtlety.
The Gate: The True Eye is ever-luminous; one is not deluded by the various sensory objects. How could one be obstructed by the emotional attachments regarding ease or difficulty?
△ Thirteen: Questioning on Past Lives.
A śramaṇa asked the Buddha, "By what causes and conditions can one know past lives and realize the ultimate Way? The Buddha said, "Purify the mind and maintain one's resolve;

thus one may realize the ultimate Way. It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is removed, the clarity remains. By severing desire and being free from seeking, one shall attain knowledge of past lives."
The mind is pure and free from desire; true wisdom is revealed. Matters of kalpas past are all known in a single thought-moment.
△ Fourteen: Inquiry Regarding What is Good and Greatest.
A śramaṇa asked the Buddha: "What is good? What is greatest? The Buddha said: "To practice the Way and maintain the truth is good."
When the will merges with the Way, one becomes great.
Practicing the Way while guarding its truth, one finds nothing to grasp among the myriad practices. When the will merges with the Way, both cultivation and realization are forgotten.
△ Fifteen: Inquiry into the Power of Illumination.
A śramaṇa asked the Buddha, "What possesses great strength? What is most luminous? The Buddha said, "Patience possesses great strength, for it harbors no ill will;
furthermore, it brings peace and well-being. One who practices patience is free from evil and shall surely become honored among men."
One who is able to practice patience may be called a powerful great person; this is something that neither the observance of precepts nor ascetic practices can equal.

There are four kinds of patience: patience in enduring suffering, patience in enduring enmity and harm, patience in the thorough investigation of dharmas, and patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.
What is here termed "endurance" (kṣānti) refers specifically to enduring enmity and harm; however, in principle, it also applies to all four types, as can be seen by reflecting upon this.
The defilements of the mind have been extinguished; it is pure and free from blemish. This is the ultimate clarity.

From before the existence of heaven and earth until this very day, throughout all the ten directions, there is nothing that is not seen, nothing that is not known, and nothing that is not heard. Thus, one attains all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).
This may be called clarity.
When the defilements of the mind are exhausted and purified, it shines alone without partiality. Possessing all-encompassing wisdom, its responses are guided by the standard.
△ Sixteen: Abandoning Attachment to Attain the Way.
The Buddha said: "When people harbor desire and do not see the Way, it is like clear water:

if one reaches down with the hand to stir it while many people stand together at its edge, none will be able to see their own reflections. Because people’s minds are turbid due to the entanglement of desire, they do not see the Way.
You śramaṇas, you should abandon desire; when the defilement of desire is exhausted, the Way can be seen."
When the water of the mind is turbid, the reflected image is obscured; when the defilements of desire are exhausted, the Way can be seen.
△ Seventeen: Light Arrives and Darkness Departs.
The Buddha said: "One who perceives the Way is like one holding a torch and entering a dark room; the darkness is immediately extinguished, and light appears."
It exists alone. When one studies the Way and perceives the Truth, ignorance is immediately extinguished, and clarity remains eternally.
Once the ignorance of deluded awakening has been extinguished, the fundamental nature of original awakening remains eternally clear.
△ The eighteen mental applications (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth are fundamentally empty.

The Buddha said: "In my Dharma, there is mindfulness without the act of mindful application; there is practice without the act of practicing; there is speech without the act of speaking; there is cultivation without the act of cultivating."
Those who understand are near; those who are deluded are far.
Thought is itself non-thought; action is itself non-action; speech is itself non-speech; cultivation is itself non-cultivation. Return to the root to attain the essential meaning;
only through realization can it be known.
The path of language is cut off; it is not constrained by material things.
The course of speech and thought is severed, and the mind of discrimination is exhausted.
To deviate by even a hair’s breadth is to lose [the truth] in an instant.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). To deliberate upon it is to fall away from it. △ Nineteen:
Contemplating the Conventional and the Real Together.
The Buddha said: "Contemplate heaven and earth, and reflect on their impermanence; contemplate the world, and reflect on its impermanence."
All conditioned phenomena ultimately return to extinction.
Contemplating the numinous awareness is itself bodhi;
this numinous cognition, quiescent and illuminating, is fundamentally the Buddha.
One who understands in this manner will swiftly attain the Way.
Awakening to the dharma of impermanence and recognizing the nature of numinous awareness, they achieve resonance in a single thought-moment; the boundaries of past and future are severed.
The illuminating essence stands alone, and both things and self are seen as suchness.
△ Twenty: Examining that the self is fundamentally empty.
The Buddha said: "One should contemplate that within the body, the four great elements each have their own names, yet there is no self at all.
That which is solid is called earth; that which is moist is called water; that which is warm is called fire; that which moves is called wind. Thus one examines and investigates these four.
Great! Their natures are each distinct. Who is "I"?
Since there is no "I" at all, it is merely like an illusion.
Knowing that the body is without self and that its arising and ceasing are like an illusion, one enters the Dharma-gate of illusion through illusory wisdom.
△ Twenty-one: Loss of One's Fundamental through Fame.
The Buddha said: "When people follow their passions and seek fame and reputation, their fame becomes prominent while their bodies have already perished.
Greedily clinging to worldly renown, they do not study the Way; thus they waste their efforts and exhaust their forms in vain."
The world prizes fame and profit, laboring in vain for their sake. If people do not study the Way, they live in emptiness and die in futility.
It is like burning incense: though others smell its fragrance, the incense itself has already been consumed. Yet the fire that endangered the body remains behind.

The greedy pursuit of fame and reputation is not only futile and profitless; by deluding oneself regarding the truth and chasing after the false, it further brings about calamities after death—how truly lamentable this is!
△ Twenty-two: Wealth and Sensual Pleasures Invite Suffering.
The Buddha said: "Wealth and sensual pleasures are such that people cannot abandon them. It is like a blade of grass smeared with honey;
it is not enough to satisfy a single meal, yet if a child licks it, he suffers the calamity of having his tongue cut."
To be attached to wealth and sensual pleasures is like licking honey from a sharp blade; one craves a small taste only to invite suffering for long kalpas.
△ Twenty-three: Wives and children are like a prison.

The Buddha said: "People are bound by their wives, children, and homes more tightly than they are by prison. While there is a time for release from prison, there is no thought of separation from one's wife and children.
When one is emotionally attached to sensual forms, how could one dread being driven to and fro?
Even when faced with the peril of a tiger’s mouth, the mind remains contentedly submissive."
A majestic man, yet driven by passions and desires, sacrifices his body and endangers his life; deluded, he does not perceive this as suffering.
Casting himself into the mud and drowning himself, he is therefore called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). One who penetrates this gate is an Arhat who has transcended the dust of the world.

To know that it is not apart from desire, yet to be an ordinary person who is not an ordinary person; to dwell amidst the dust of the world without being stained by it—this is an Arhat who has transcended the mundane.
△ Twenty-four: Sensual Desire Obstructs the Path.
The Buddha said: "Among all forms of craving, none is more profound than that for form. As for the desire for form, it is so vast that there is nothing beyond its reach.
Regarding the afflictions and calamities of craving, they take many forms; yet in obstructing the Path and fostering evil, nothing is more extreme than the beauty of women."
Fortunately, there is but one [obstacle]. If there were two equal [obstacles], then no person throughout the heavens would be able to practice the Way;
it would only increase birth and death and obstruct nirvana, with the single factor of desire for form and desire for sensual pleasure being the sole hindrance. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* also says:
"If the lustful mind is not eliminated, one cannot transcend the dusts of the world."
△ Twenty-fifth: The Fire of Desire Burns the Body.
The Buddha said: "A person driven by craving and desire is like one who holds a torch while walking against the wind; they will inevitably suffer the calamity of burning their hands."
To go against the wind of the objective realm while clutching the torch of ignorance—how could one avoid being consumed by its own flames?
△ Twenty-six: The Heavenly Demons Disturb the Buddha.
A celestial deity presented jade maidens to the Buddha, seeking to corrupt his resolve.
When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, the celestial Mara Pāpīyas attempted to disturb him with jade maidens.
The Buddha said: "A leather bag filled with various impurities—what is the purpose of your coming? Begone; I have no need for you."
When people see the beauty of women, they falsely give rise to thoughts of purity and thus develop defiled attachment; they do not know that it is fundamentally impure, merely wrapped in thin skin.
The heavenly deity, increasingly respectful, asked about the meaning of the Way. The Buddha explained it for him, and he immediately attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
Māra could find no opportunity. He turned from the heterodox to the orthodox, sought the Way, attained enlightenment, and realized the first fruit of the Lesser Vehicle.
△ Twenty-seventh: Wuzhuo attains the Way.
The Buddha said: "One who practices the Way is like a piece of wood floating in water, following the current as it flows.
It does not touch either bank; it is not taken by people; it is not obstructed by ghosts or spirits; it is not held back by eddies; nor does it rot.
I guarantee that this wood will certainly reach the sea."
They do not touch the two shores of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; they are not grasped by the tainted wholesome karma of humans or devas;
they are not obstructed by spirits of false views; they do not dwell within the whirlpools of the triple world;
nor do they become corrupted by the extinction-concentration of the two vehicles. They resolutely enter the ocean of sarvajñā.
One who studies the Way is not deluded by emotional desires and is not harassed by various evils;
being diligent and non-active, I guarantee that such a person will surely attain the Way.
Passions cannot delude them; manifold evils cannot harass them. They advance rightly toward non-action. Is the Way far away? △ Twenty-eighth:
Do not let the horse of the mind run wild.
The Buddha said: "Be careful not to trust your own mind; your mind is not to be trusted. Be careful not to associate with forms (*rūpa*); when one associates with forms, calamity arises.
The horse of the mind is difficult to tame; the precepts serve as its bridle and reins. When one is defiled by the habituation of sensual desire, the Way is ruined and the body is lost."
Only after attaining arhatship can one truly believe in the nature of your mind;
when the faculty of mind is extinguished, one realizes arhatship. Long ago, there was a practitioner in the Western Regions who cultivated his practice in the mountains.

He attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). One day, because of rain and mud, he slipped and fell. Thereupon, by the power of his incantations (*dhāraṇī*), he caused it not to rain for twelve years.
When the king learned that this was due to the power of the practitioner’s incantations, he became filled with grief and issued an edict stating:
"If there is anyone who can subdue this practitioner, I shall reward them with a thousand *jin* of gold. A courtesan came forward and addressed the king, saying:
"I shall be able to subdue him. Your Majesty, permit me to go there to pay homage to that practitioner, touch his body, and thereby give rise to a mind of passion;
thus he will lose his supernormal powers. Then, as torrential rain poured down, the woman mounted the practitioner's neck and came before the king.
The King then praised and rewarded him. Thus we know that the ruin of the Way and the loss of one’s resolve stem from the calamity of female beauty. How can one not be cautious?
How can one not be cautious?
△ Twenty-nine: Rightly Contemplating the Appearance of the Enemy.
The Buddha said: "Be careful not to look upon the beauty of women, nor speak with them.
To become intimate and give rise to passion leads to the loss of right mindfulness.
If you must speak with them, maintain a correct mind and reflect: 'I am a śramaṇa dwelling in a turbid world; I should be like a lotus flower.'"
One shall not be defiled by mud. One should regard the elderly as one's mother, the elders as elder sisters, the young as younger sisters, and the children as one's own offspring;
thus generating a mind intent on deliverance and extinguishing all evil thoughts.
Observe with right mindfulness; let the mind be pure and the intellect liberated. Though born and dwelling in a turbid world, be like a lotus flower emerging from the water.
Through skillful means and mental visualization as an antidote, contemplate that all sentient beings wandering in saṃsāra since beginningless time have all been one's own kin.
Vowing to deliver them all, evil thoughts and conceptions will naturally subside and cease.
△ Thirty: Avoidance of the Fire of Desire.
The Buddha said: "One who practices the Way is like dry grass; when fire approaches, it must be avoided. When a practitioner of the Way encounters desire, he must certainly distance himself from it."
Emotional defilement is like dry reeds; the fire of desire should be kept far away.
△ Thirty-first: Calming the Mind to Eliminate Desire.
The Buddha said: There was a man who suffered from incessant lust and wished to remove his own genitals himself. The Buddha said to him: "If you were to cut off your genitals..."
It is better to sever the mind.
Since delusions arise from the mind, they merely cause injury to the body.
The mind is like a chief minister; if the chief minister stops, all his followers will come to rest.
The army follows the turning of the seal; the general proceeds according to the talisman.
If the evil mind does not cease, what benefit is there in severing the *skandhas*? The Buddha spoke this verse for him: "Desire arises within your mind;
the mind arises from conceptualization. When both minds are each stilled, they are neither form nor mental formations."
Since his mind is already tranquil and delusive thoughts do not arise, the five aggregates are fundamentally empty; how could desire and passion arise?
The Buddha said: "This verse was spoken by Kāśyapa Buddha."
He cites a verse from the Buddha as clear proof:
"Thirty-two: The Fear of Self-Emptiness is Extinguished.
The Buddha said: "Man gives rise to sorrow through craving; from sorrow arises fear. If one is free from craving, what sorrow and what fear can there be?"

Sentient beings delusively identify the four great elements as their own bodies. When things accord with their desires, they give rise to attachment; when they oppose their desires, they give rise to grief. Thus, there are five kinds of fear:
namely, the fear of lacking a livelihood, the fear of ill repute, the fear of the majesty of the great assembly, the fear of death, and the fear of falling into the evil realms.
If one can awaken to the fact that the self is fundamentally empty, then such discrimination will suddenly cease. Who, then, would be subject to attachment?
What, then, is there to fear? △ Thirty-third:
The Radiance of Wisdom Destroys Mara.
The Buddha said: "Now, one who practices the Way is like a single person going out to battle ten thousand men; having donned his armor and stepped forth from the gate, his mind might—"
They may be timid and weak; they may retreat halfway; they may die in combat; or they may return victorious.

A śramaṇa who studies the Way should firmly maintain his mind, exerting himself with vigor and sharpness, not fearing the objects before him, destroying all demons, and thereby attaining the fruits of the Way.

When a practitioner of the Way battles against the various māras, they should don the armor of pure precepts, maintain the mind of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wield the sword of wisdom (*prajñā*).
When not a single dharma can stir the passions, one shatters the māras and achieves victory. This is also as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*:

"One sees the army of sages and saints battling the māra of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-māra*), the māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), and the māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*); having achieved great merit, they extinguish the three poisons."
Having emerged from the three realms and shattered the net of Māra, at that time the Tathāgata was also greatly rejoiced; the meaning is the same as this.
△ Thirty-fourth: Attaining the Way within a location.

A śramaṇa was reciting the *Kāśyapa-buddha-śāsana-sūtra* at night; his voice was mournful and strained, and he was filled with regret and a desire to withdraw. The Buddha asked him, "When you were formerly a householder, what was your occupation? He replied, "I loved to play the lute. The Buddha said, "If the strings are too loose, what happens? He replied, "They do not sound. "If the strings are too tight, what happens? He replied, "The sound is broken. "When they are neither too tight nor too loose, but find the middle, [what happens? He replied, "Then the sounds are harmonious and beautiful. The Buddha said, "It is the same for the mind. If it is too lax, one falls into negligence; if it is too tense, one falls into agitation. You must practice with right mindfulness, keeping the mind in the middle, free from both laxity and tension. Upon hearing this, the śramaṇa attained the fruit of arhatship. The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus: "This śramaṇa has already practiced the path under twenty-nine Buddhas, yet he did not attain the fruit. It is only because he encountered Kāśyapa Buddha that he has now realized the Way. The Buddha further told the bhikṣus: "If there is a person who, having heard the Dharma, attains the fruit of arhatship, know that such a person has long cultivated the roots of goodness. Why is this? Because the Dharma is difficult to encounter, and the arising of a Buddha is rare. Therefore, you should all diligently cultivate the path, so as not to be like those who, though having met a Buddha, fail to attain the fruit. The Buddha then spoke this verse: "The Dharma is difficult to encounter, And the arising of a Buddha is rare. One who hears the Dharma and attains the fruit Has surely practiced the path in former lives. The Buddha then told the bhikṣus: "In the past, there was a king named Śubhavyūha. He had a son named Candraprabha, who was wise and virtuous. When the prince grew up, he took pleasure in the arts and sciences. One day, the king summoned a master luthier and said, 'I wish to have a lute made for my son. The luthier replied, 'As Your Majesty commands. Having received the order, he went to the mountains and forests to seek out the finest materials. After much searching, he found a tree of exquisite quality and returned to present it to the king. The king then ordered the prince to have the lute crafted. The prince said, 'I am but a youth; I do not yet understand the principles of music. I beg you to let the master himself fashion it. The master said, 'Very well. He then began to work on the instrument. First, he tuned the strings. As he adjusted them, he thought: 'If the strings are too loose, the sound will be dull; if they are too tight, the sound will snap. Only when they are perfectly balanced can the music be harmonious. He then applied this principle to the cultivation of the mind, realizing that the mind, too, requires balance between laxity and tension. Having understood this, he immediately left the palace, renounced the world, and became a śramaṇa. Under the guidance of a spiritual friend, he practiced diligently and soon attained arhatship. The Buddha said, "That master luthier was none other than this very śramaṇa. Because he understood the principle of tuning the lute, he was able to realize the Way upon hearing the Dharma today. The Buddha then told the bhikṣus: "If you wish to attain liberation, you must cultivate the mind with right mindfulness, avoiding the extremes of laxity and tension. This is the true path to awakening. Thus the Buddha spoke. All the bhikṣus, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, rejoiced and put it into practice. They all attained the fruit of arhatship. The World-Honored One then rose from his seat and departed. The assembly followed him, their minds filled with joy. This concludes the *Sūtra on the Lute*, the thirteenth chapter. "What is it? he asked. He replied, "All sounds are pervasive. The Buddha said, "It is the same for a śramaṇa who studies the Way.

If the mind is harmonized and at ease, the Way can be attained. If one is violent toward the Way, that violence will lead to physical exhaustion. If the body is exhausted, the mind will give rise to affliction.
If the mind gives rise to affliction, one's practice will regress. Once practice has regressed, retribution must surely follow. Therefore, one should simply remain pure, serene, and at peace."
The Way will not be lost.
One who studies the Way skillfully employs their mind: neither hurried nor slow, not stagnating in emptiness within, nor grasping at signs without;
above, there is no reaching up in longing, and below, one cuts off attachment to the self. Thus, being pure and tranquil, one’s practice may advance. This is the Way.
It can be attained. △ Thirty-fifth: The Clarity of Defilement and Purity.

The Buddha said: "It is like a person forging iron; by removing the dross, it is formed into a vessel. Once the vessel is made, it is refined and excellent. So too is it for one who studies the Way: they must remove the mind's [defilements]."
Defiled conduct is itself purification.
To create karma by following one's passions is called defilement; to advance in practice in accordance with principle is termed purification.
△ Thirty-six: Attaining Superiority through Successive Progression.
The Buddha said: "It is difficult for a person to escape the evil realms and obtain human birth. Having obtained human birth, it is difficult to be male rather than female.

Having obtained male status, it is difficult for the six sense faculties to be complete. Once the five faculties are complete, it is difficult to be born in a central land. Having been born in a central land,"
It is difficult to encounter the era of a Buddha. Having encountered the era of a Buddha, it is difficult to meet with the Way. Having met with the Way, it is difficult to give rise to faith.
Having given rise to faith, it is difficult to resolve upon the Bodhicitta. Having resolved upon the Bodhicitta, it is difficult to practice without cultivation and realize without attainment.

The preceding twenty difficulties have not yet discussed the arousal of the bodhicitta. From the present departure from the evil realms up to the state of neither cultivation nor realization, the beginning and end of spiritual practice have been briefly exhausted.
Although one may have planted roots of goodness in past lives and cultivated the myriad practices over time, the arousal of the vast mind is truly rare.
Nevertheless, I fear that expectations may still persist and the grasping and rejecting of phenomena remain unextinguished, bound by even a hair’s breadth.
If mindfulness still results in the achievement of a state of abiding, and if even a fleeting emotion arises, one falls into the rank of cultivation and realization.
Therefore, it concludes by stating "no cultivation, no realization," so as not to fall into the realm of meritorious achievement; this alone is called the most difficult of difficulties.
△ Thirty-seven recollections of the precepts bring one near to the Way.
The Buddha said: "A son of the Buddha who is thousands of li away from me, yet constantly recollects my precepts, will surely attain the fruit of the Way.
One who is at my side and constantly sees me, yet does not comply with my precepts, will ultimately not attain the Way."

To be near the Buddha while violating the precepts does not exempt one from the cycle of saṃsāra; to remember the precepts while remaining distant from the Buddha leads to the attainment of the Way and the realization of the fruit.
△ Thirty-eight lifetimes pass and there is still extinction.
The Buddha asked a śramaṇa, "In how much time does a person's life reside? He replied, "In several days. The Buddha said, "You do not yet know the Way."
He again asked another śramaṇa: "In what interval does a person's life reside? He replied: "In the interval of a meal.

The Buddha said: "You do not yet know the Way. He again asked another śramaṇa: "In what interval does a person's life reside? He replied: "In the interval of a single breath. The Buddha said: "Excellent!"
My son, you understand this.
That which sustains the uninterrupted functional capacity of the eighth consciousness, induced by karma, is called "life. An ordinary person has ninety *kṣaṇas* in a single thought-moment;
each *kṣaṇa* contains nine hundred births and cessations. Moment after moment they pass away and perish, yet one remains unaware and unconscious of it.
How could one possibly awaken to and understand the Way of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness?
△ Thirty-ninth: The Ocean of Teachings is Without Difference.
The Buddha said: "Those who study the Buddha-way should believe and comply with all that the Buddha has spoken. It is like eating honey; [it is sweet] from the center to the edges."
All are sweet. My sutras are likewise:
the ocean of the teaching is of a single flavor, yet it manifests in ten thousand differences according to individual capacities.

Those who believe, comply, and practice will all leave suffering behind and attain happiness—just as when eating honey, both the center and the edges are sweet; or like drinking from the ocean, where all beings, great and small, are fully satiated.
△ Forty: Walking the Path Resides in the Mind.
The Buddha said: "When a śramaṇa walks the path, there is none like a 'grinding ox. Though the body walks the path, the mind does not walk the path.
If the mind were to walk the path, what need would there be for the body to walk the path?"
The four modes of deportment—moving and stopping—are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing. The mind is fundamentally unborn; it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating.
One who realizes this principle is truly practicing the Way.
△ Forty-first: Rectitude of Mind Eliminates Desire.
The Buddha said: "One who practices the Way is like an ox carrying a heavy load through deep mud; exhausted, it does not dare look left or right.
Only after emerging from the mire can it find rest. A śramaṇa should contemplate that sensual desire is even more perilous than that mud."
By maintaining a straightforward mind and contemplating the Way, one may escape suffering.
The deep mire of the five desires is perilous for those who sink into it; if one does not maintain a straightforward mind and contemplate the Way, by what means can one achieve liberation?
△ Forty-second: Reaching the World’s Knowledge of Illusion.
The Buddha said: "I regard the rank of kings and lords as a speck of dust passing through a crevice;
it is restless and never still, appearing to exist yet lacking reality."
One regards treasures of gold and jade as mere tiles and pebbles;
though accumulated in heights like mountains, they are of no benefit to the Way.
One regards garments of fine silk as worn-out rags.
Using clothing merely to conceal the body, one does not seek out ornaments or finery.
One views the great trichiliocosm as being like a single *harītakī* fruit;

though the vastness of the great trichiliocosm and the environmental retributions upon which sentient beings depend are formed by the collective karma of impure wholesome dharmas, one contemplates them thus.
It is like a *hing* fruit; originally it was but small. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Emptiness arises within Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble surfacing upon the ocean.
The minute dust-motes of the realms of outflows are all produced dependent upon emptiness. When the bubble ceases, emptiness is fundamentally non-existent;
how much more so the various realms of the three worlds?"
One views the waters of Lake Anavatapta as if they were oil for anointing the feet.
"Anavatapta" is translated in the Song language as "Free from Heat and Torment. It is named after its dragon; the lake is deep and vast.
Compared to the depth and vastness of this lake, the ocean of wisdom is like a mere drop.
Viewing the gates of skillful means as a conjured heap of jewels,
they manifest the wealth of the Dharma to relieve all who are destitute;
viewing the Unsurpassed Vehicle as gold and silk in a dream.
He guides those who have not yet awakened, causing them to give rise to faith and joy.
He regards the Buddha-way as a flower before one's eyes;
responding to conditions according to their capacity, he realizes that [all things] are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning.
He regards meditative concentration as Mount Sumeru,
which cannot be shaken by the winds of sensory objects or the waves of consciousness.
He regards nirvana as waking from sleep at dawn.
Perfect stillness and illuminating eternity are free from all dreams and thoughts.
Viewing the inverted and the upright is like the dance of six dragons;

as the six dragons ascend and descend, they are fundamentally neither upright nor inverted. It is through following deluded perceptions and attachments that the notions of "upright" and "inverted" arise. If one understands this seeing...
Delusion! Who is right and who is inverted?
View all things as equal, as the single true ground, the ground of ultimate reality, where not even a single speck of dust can be received.
Observe the flourishing of the Xinghua [Blossoms]: they are like the trees of the four seasons.
This is the method of cosmic transformation; throughout antiquity and the present, things undergo change through birth, abiding, alteration, and extinction—spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

It is because of the karmic conditions of sentient beings that there arise the appearances of flourishing, withering, decay, and prosperity. If one understands this inconceivable dependent origination, one attains liberation.
Regarding the Dharma-gate of liberation: one thereby knows that arising is merely the arising of dharmas, and cessation is merely the cessation of dharmas.
One must believe that when the kalpa-fire blazes forth, even the finest hairs are consumed; yet the green mountains remain as before amidst the white clouds.
Annotated Commentary on the Sutra of Forty-two Sections Spoken by the Buddha (End)
